title: Customers With Strictly Increasing Purchases
statement:
One table records customers' orders:

- `Orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, price)`: one row per order; `order_id` is unique, `order_date` is a date and `price` is a positive integer. A customer may place several orders in a year, even on the same day.

A customer's **total purchases** in a year is the sum of `price` over their orders dated in that year. Look at every calendar year from the year of the customer's first order to the year of their last order, inclusive; a year in that span with no orders counts as a total of `0`.

Report the `customer_id` of every customer whose yearly totals are **strictly increasing** across that span (each year's total is greater than the previous year's). A customer whose orders all fall in one year qualifies. Rows may come in any order.
reference:
WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS yr, SUM(price) AS total
  FROM Orders
  GROUP BY customer_id, YEAR(order_date)
),
compared AS (
  SELECT customer_id, yr, total,
         LAG(yr) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_yr,
         LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_total
  FROM yearly
)
SELECT customer_id
FROM compared
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN prev_yr IS NULL THEN 0
                WHEN yr = prev_yr + 1 AND total > prev_total THEN 0
                ELSE 1 END) = 0;
brute:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS yr, SUM(price) AS total
  FROM Orders
  GROUP BY customer_id, YEAR(order_date)
)
SELECT a.customer_id
FROM totals AS a
LEFT JOIN totals AS b
  ON b.customer_id = a.customer_id AND b.yr = a.yr + 1
GROUP BY a.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) - COUNT(b.yr) = 1
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN b.total <= a.total THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0
notes:
## Intuition

The rule is about **yearly totals**, not single orders, so the first stage collapses orders into one row per customer and year. A customer then qualifies when, walking through their years in order, each year is exactly one after the previous and has a larger total. A missing year in the middle has total 0, and since prices are positive the year before it always had more than 0, so any gap is a failure. Comparing each year with the one before it is a job for `LAG`.

## Approach

1. `yearly`: `GROUP BY customer_id, YEAR(order_date)` and `SUM(price)` give `total` per customer and year `yr`.
2. `compared`: `LAG` over each customer's years in order brings the previous year (`prev_yr`) and its total (`prev_total`) onto the row.
3. Final select: a row is bad unless it is the first year (`prev_yr` is null) or it directly follows the previous year with a larger total. `GROUP BY customer_id` and keep customers whose bad-row count is 0.

## Example 1, step by step

| customer_id | yr | total | prev_yr | prev_total | bad |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2019 | 2300 | null | null | 0 |
| 1 | 2020 | 3000 | 2019 | 2300 | 0 |
| 1 | 2021 | 3100 | 2020 | 3000 | 0 |
| 1 | 2022 | 4700 | 2021 | 3100 | 0 |
| 2 | 2015 | 700 | null | null | 0 |
| 2 | 2017 | 1000 | 2015 | 700 | 1 (2016 is missing) |
| 3 | 2017 | 900 | null | null | 0 |
| 3 | 2018 | 900 | 2017 | 900 | 1 (not larger) |

Only customer 1 has no bad rows, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for n orders, for the grouping and the window sort.
- Space: O(n) for the yearly rows.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing individual orders instead of yearly sums: customer 1's two 2019 orders must be added first.
- Ignoring gap years: customer 2 looks increasing (700, 1000) unless the missing 2016 is treated as 0.
- `>=` instead of `>` lets equal totals through, like customer 3.
- Dropping first-year rows with `WHERE prev_yr IS NOT NULL` would also drop single-year customers, who must be reported.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `yearly` | one row per customer and year with its `total` |
| `compared` | each yearly row with the previous year's `prev_yr` and `prev_total` |
| `yr` | the calendar year of the orders |
| `HAVING SUM(CASE ...) = 0` | the customer has no year that breaks the rule |

narration.1: The first stage turns orders into one row per customer and year.
narration.2: Sum the prices of each customer's orders that fall in the same calendar year.
narration.4: Group by customer and year so each yearly total is computed separately.
narration.6: The second stage puts each year next to the customer's previous year.
narration.8: LAG reads the previous year number in the customer's year order, or null for the first year.
narration.9: LAG reads the previous year's total so the two totals can be compared on one row.
narration.12: Each qualifying customer is reported once by id.
narration.14: Group the yearly rows by customer so their years can be judged together.
narration.15: Count the bad years: any year that does not directly follow the previous one with a larger total.
narration.17: Keep a customer only if that count is 0; the first year never counts as bad.
